system:
You audit the knowledge atoms of one Knowledge Card. A card is the answer key for a benchmark of expert conceptual knowledge, so every atom must be correct, self-contained, and assessable on its own.

Judge every atom on every check listed below. Rules:
- For checks about evidence, use only the evidence sentences supplied with the atom. Do not repair an atom with your own knowledge.
- Evidence text comes from a PDF text layer. If symbols are garbled so that you cannot verify the atom, answer "hold" for that check and say so.
- Be strict. When unsure between pass and a non-pass value, choose the non-pass value and explain.
- "why" is required for every value other than the first listed value; keep it under 30 words. Omit "why" when passing.

Checks (allowed values in brackets; the first value means no problem):
- GROUNDED [pass / revise / fail]: The cited evidence sentences state the atom. pass = fully stated. revise = the core claim is stated, and the gap is only wording, strength, or a dropped/extra peripheral qualifier that can be fixed by deleting or softening words (say what). fail = not stated, OR the atom adds substantive content the evidence lacks: a scope or population restriction (e.g. 'In B-ALL'), a mechanism or operation, a characterization (e.g. 'an unbounded while loop'), or a formula/definition. If deleting the unsupported part would change what the atom tests, it is fail, not revise. For pass, put the supporting evidence ids in cite (required).
- SINGLE_CLAIM [pass / revise]: The atom is one independently assessable claim. revise = it joins two or more claims that could be true or false separately.
- SCOPE_LABEL [pass / revise]: The S label fits (S1 what it is / S2 how it works / S3 where it ends). revise = wrong label; put the right one in why, e.g. 'S2: ...'.
- L1_ONLY [pass / revise / fail]: The atom is recall-level knowledge: one fact a person who studied the concept would simply know. revise = the core fact is recall-level but the sentence carries extra load that must be removed, e.g. stacked conditions (since/although/if ... and ...), a procedural or evaluative add-on ('easy to define but requires checking ...'), or a clause that introduces a second technical concept that must be known separately (e.g. 'if X is an inner Kan complex' when that is not the card concept). fail = knowing it requires applying the concept to a new problem, or combining facts from distant passages.
- SOURCE_INDEPENDENT [pass / revise / fail]: A domain expert who never read this book could judge the claim true or false. revise = phrased as the authors' statement but the claim itself is general (drop the attribution). fail = the authors' opinion or choice, or the finding of one study, so the answer is not fixed without the source.
- NO_OVERLAP [pass / fail]: No other atom in this card states or contains the same claim. If two atoms overlap, fail only the less informative one and put the other atom's id in cite; the other one passes.
- CENTRALITY [pass / fail]: The atom matters for understanding the concept. fail = peripheral detail.
Whole-card checks (report under "batch"):
- CONCEPT_SCOPE [pass / fail]: The concept is a general concept of the field. fail = a single system, product, or one study's topic.

Output ONLY one JSON object:
{"units": {"<atom_id>": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": "", "cite": []}, ...}, ...}, "batch": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": ""}}}

CONCEPT: Kernel bundles
ASSESSMENT SCOPE: Covers kernel bundles as containers for kernels, their input/object/executable states, lazy JIT compilation and its first-use cost, explicit compilation, and kernel queries needing named kernels. Excludes backend-specific kernel creation.

ATOMS:
- DPCPP2-C10-S1-01 | S1
  ATOM: A SYCL kernel bundle is a container for the SYCL kernels or SYCL functions used by an application.
  EVIDENCE:
    [DPCPP2-p0285-s05] A SYCL kernel bundle is a container for SYCL kernels or SYCL
    [DPCPP2-p0285-s06] functions used by an application.
- DPCPP2-C10-S1-02 | S1
  ATOM: A SYCL kernel bundle, together with the kernels or functions it contains, can be in one of three states: input, object, or executable.
  EVIDENCE:
    [DPCPP2-p0285-s09] A SYCL kernel bundle and the kernels or functions it contains can be in
    [DPCPP2-p0285-s10] one of three states:
- DPCPP2-C10-S1-03 | S1
  ATOM: A kernel bundle in the executable state is fully compiled to device code and is ready to be executed on the device.
  EVIDENCE:
    [DPCPP2-p0285-s13] • An executable state: Kernel bundles in this state are fully compiled to device code and are ready to be executed on the device.
- DPCPP2-C10-S2-01 | S2
  ATOM: Many SYCL runtime libraries compile kernel bundles from the input state to the executable state lazily, on an as-needed basis, which enables fast application startup and avoids compiling kernels that are never executed.
  EVIDENCE:
    [DPCPP2-p0286-s04] Then, many SYCL runtime libraries compile the kernel bundles from the input state to the executable state “lazily,” on an as-needed basis.
    [DPCPP2-p0286-s05] This is usually a good policy because it enables fast application startup
    [DPCPP2-p0286-s06] and does not compile kernels unnecessarily if they are never executed.
- DPCPP2-C10-S2-02 | S2
  ATOM: Under lazy just-in-time compilation, the first use of a kernel takes longer than later uses because it includes both the kernel compile time and the usual time to submit and execute the kernel.
  EVIDENCE:
    [DPCPP2-p0286-s07] The disadvantage of this policy, though, is that the first use of a kernel takes longer than subsequent uses, since it includes both the time needed to compile the kernel and the usual time needed to submit and execute the kernel.
- DPCPP2-C10-S2-03 | S2
  ATOM: Requesting a kernel bundle in the executable state for all devices in the context associated with a SYCL queue causes any kernels not already in the executable state to be just-in-time compiled, shifting compilation to that explicit point.
  EVIDENCE:
    [DPCPP2-p0287-s02] This example requests a kernel bundle in an executable state for all
    [DPCPP2-p0287-s03] the devices in the SYCL context associated with the SYCL queue, which will cause any kernels in the application to be just-in-time compiled if they are not already in the executable state.
- DPCPP2-C10-S3-01 | S3
  ATOM: The number of kernel bundles in an application depends on the specific SYCL compiler, so an application with multiple kernels may have just one bundle while one with a few kernels may have more than one.
  EVIDENCE:
    [DPCPP2-p0285-s07] The number of kernel bundles in an application depends on the specific SYCL compiler.
    [DPCPP2-p0285-s08] Some applications may have just one kernel bundle, even if they have multiple kernels, while other applications may have more than one kernel bundle, even if they just have a few kernels.
- DPCPP2-C10-S3-02 | S3
  ATOM: Explicitly requesting an executable-state kernel bundle is effectively free if all kernels were ahead-of-time compiled or were already just-in-time compiled, because all kernels would already be in the executable state.
  EVIDENCE:
    [DPCPP2-p0287-s05] Of course, if all kernels were ahead-of-time compiled, or if all kernels had already been just-in-time compiled, this operation would effectively be free because all kernels would already be in the executable state.
- DPCPP2-C10-S3-03 | S3
  ATOM: Querying a kernel, for example for its preferred_work_group_size_multiple via get_info(), requires an instance of the kernel class, which requires knowing the kernel's name and kernel_id to extract it from the kernel_bundle, so the kernel lambda must be named.
  EVIDENCE:
    [DPCPP2-p0370-s05] We also need to name kernels if we want to use kernel queries.
    [DPCPP2-p0370-s08] For instance, querying a kernel’s preferred_work_group_size_multiple requires us to call the get_info() member function of the kernel class, which requires an instance of the kernel class, which ultimately requires that we know the name (and kernel_id) of the kernel in order to extract a handle to it from the relevant kernel_bundle.
